item.title: The humble for loop in Rust
item.description:
Score 90 | Comments 54 (thread link) | @todsacerdoti
December 12, 2024 | https://blog.startifact.com/posts/humble-for-loop-rust/ | archive.org

Rust has some really nice functional programming facilities built in, all around an iterator concept. Rust being focused on performance and low level control makes it possible to use this without paying a performance cost. Sometimes I still prefer to use the humble for loop though. In quite a few cases, it combines high performance with high readability. I thought I'd motivate why.

I've written previously (um, well, today) about the humble for loop in JavaScript, and I think heuristics involved carry across languages that have collection data structures like vectors and hashmaps (JavaScript arrays, object/HashMap, Python lists and dictionaries). Let's see how this works out in Rust. But even if you're not an expert in Rust you should be able to follow most of it, as I explain Rust concepts along the way.

This being about Rust, I'm going to give some performance numbers in this article. The precise details of these numbers don't really matter. They will be different depending on what data you're working with. For the purposes of this article, whenever there's merely a percentage difference in performance, that's relatively unimportant. Where it gets interesting is when I start to talk about 3, 10, or a 100 times faster, as these demonstrate real algorithmic differences that hold up in many contexts, and therefore can help guide our behavior.

Map

Let's consider a transform loop first.

let mut result = Vec::new();
for entry in list {
    result.push(transform(entry));
}

It's almost identical to examples you'd see in JavaScript or Python. Vec is an expandable array in Rust, like a JavaScript array or Python list.

The simple loop has good performance, but this is actually faster, by about 30% for a bunch of i32 numbers 1:

let mut result = Vec::with_capacity(list.len());
for entry in list {
    result.push(transform(entry));
}

The way Vec works (just like in Python and JS) is that it preallocates space in advance, so that every push does not require a memory reallocation (which requires copying the data, which is expensive). But since it doesn't know how big the final array will be, it may not be able to avoid reallocation entirely.

Here we avoid reallocations altogether by giving it the final amount right away using with_capacity(); we know it's going to be identical in length to the input list.

Now let's look at map().

let result: Vec<i32> = list.into_iter().map(transform).collect()

A few explanations are in order:

  • into_iter() turns the original vector into an iterator. The for loop uses into_iter() too, but implicitly.

  • map() does not return a vector, unlike in Javascript where it produces an array. Instead it returns an iterator (that has the mapping operation built-in). Calling map() does not actually take much time at all as it's constructing an iterator, not executing it.

  • collect() takes an iterator and turns it back into a vector. This is going to do the actual work.

I think we can agree that map() in Rust is pretty readable. While there are a few more concepts invovled that you don't need to understand when you use a for loop, these concepts are so fundamental to Rust you're going to have to learn them anyway. So .map() wins in being more declarative.

Surprisingly enough, map() can also be a lot faster. On a loop of 10000 integers it's 6 times faster on my machine!

Why is map so much faster? I am not sure. I suspect with the map() option the Rust compiler figures out it can avoid allocations altogether by simply writing over the original vector, while with the loop it can't. Or maybe it's using SIMD? I tried to look in the compiler explorer but I'm not competent enough yet to figure it out. Maybe someone else can explain! 2

This is a great argument to use functional programming patterns when they're simple! More declarative and more fast? Let's use it!

Fold (Reduce)

In JavaScript we saw that a for loop for constructing a new collection was orders of magnitude faster than using reduce, but does the same apply to Rust? After all, map() is so good! Does this mean that with Rust we should use fold (which is the equivalent of reduce in Rust) rather than a for loop too?

Let's look at implementing flatten, the example I also used in my JavaScript post. Here's the simple for loop:

let mut flat = Vec::new();
for entry in list_of_lists {
    flat.extend(entry);
}

extend() a way to push a whole lot of items at once, like you have in Python. 3

Note that we can't really do much with preallocated capacity here as we don't know the total length of the flattened list in advance, so we don't bother.

Here's the fold version closest to the one we used in JavaScript:

let flat = list_of_lists.into_iter().fold(Vec::new(), 
  |accumulator, list| [accumulator, list].concat()
);

Let's pick this one apart:

  • We use fold(). Rust does have a reduce() but fold is the closest equivalent to JavaScript reduce. It doesn't matter in performance.

  • |accumulator, list| ... is a closure, a function we pass in much like we do in JS.

  • [accumulator, list].concat() is a way to add two vectors together to create a new vector.

The simple for loop is about 180 times faster for this approach (for a list of 50,000 items after flattening).

If you're a Rust developer, you might object. This approach is terrible! It allocates memory all over the place, no wonder it's slower.

But in Rust we can avoid instantiating vectors all over place as we have iterators. Let's try this on the iterator level:

let flat = list_of_lists.into_iter().fold(Vec::new(), |accumulator, list| {
    accumulator.into_iter().chain(list).collect()
});

What's going on here? We use .chain() to combine the accumulator iterator with the list iterator, and then we collect it.

Does this help? Not really -- it's faster than the concat version by only 20% or so; not even close to the for loop.

Whoah, wait. We're still actually constructing vectors all over the place here, as we collect inside the closure!

Can we avoid this and just create iterators and finally collect them in the end?

let iter: Box<dyn Iterator<Item = i32>> = Box::new(std::iter::empty());
let flat = list_of_lists.into_iter()
    .fold(iter, |accumulator, list| Box::new(accumulator.chain(list)))
    .collect()

Yes we can, but we can already see this is a lot harder to read, and it actually makes it more than 10 times slower! I'm not entirely sure why - apparently the overhead of constructing chained iterators and heap allocation kills performance.

If you're new to Rust, sorry. The Box<dyn Iterator<Item = i32>> stuff is to tell Rust to use dynamic dispatch so I can combine the empty iterator we start with iterators based on the chain. These have different types in Rust and this is the way to make them go together.

Is there then no declarative way in Rust to express this and still have performance? I mean, besides .flatten() which Rust has as well? We can use flat_map:

let flat = list_of_lists.into_iter().flat_map(|list| list).collect()

flat_map lets you map but also produce structure, which then immediately gets flattened. This is a lot faster than our concat approach, but still 4 times slower than the for loop. 4

So the pattern holds: the humble for loop, even in Rust, is worth your consideration. Use fold() if it makes your code easier to write, not because it's necessarily faster.

Errors and map

It's common in code for an operation to fail and we want to handle such failures. Instead of using exceptions like many programming languages, Rust has a very nice system for propagating error values just like you propagate any return value. I won't go into the details here, but hopefully you can follow along.

Let's consider map() again, but with errors.

struct Error;

fn transform(entry: Entry) -> Result<Transformed, Error> {
    // do stuff to create a Transformed from Entry. It might fail
}

fn transform_list(list: Vec<Entry>) -> Result<Vec<Transformed>, Error> {
    let mut result = Vec::with_capacity(list.len());
    for entry in list {
        result.push(transform(entry)?);
    }
    result
}

We can see that the transform function returns a Result, which is either a Transformed object (success!) or or an error (some object describing the error).

Since transform is fallible, transform_list is also fallible and thus needs to return Result too. We either get a list that was successfully transformed, or an error.

As soon as we have an error, we want to bail out with it. That's what the ? operator after transform(entry)? does; it is equivalent to an if statement that checks whether the value evaluated is an error, and if so, it immediately returns from the function using the error value.

What does this look like with map()?

fn transform_list(list: Vec<Entry>) -> Result<Vec<Transformed>, Error> {
    list.into_iter().map(transform).collect()
}

This is functionally equivalent to the above, believe it or not. First we turn the list into an iterator, so we can iterate through all the values in it. Then we use the functional map with the transform function. Then we collect it back into a vector. You'd expect that to be Vec<Result<Transformed>, Error>; a list of results - either values or error objects.

But since we have declared the return value of the function to be Result<Vec<Transformed>, Error> a different collect is selected that short-circuits and bails out with an error as soon as the first one is found, just like in the for loop.

And what about with_capacity? We don't need it, because the implementation is smart enough to ask the iterator whether it has a size hint for that, and since it's based on a vector with a known length, it has one.

So we get a lot of cleverness for free.

More complex error handling

Again we learn that map() is great! Use map()! Sometimes however the for loop makes error handling a lot more convenient. Some things are just difficult to capture in a pattern that's both efficient and declarative. Let's consider a fallible flatten.

pub fn fallible_flatten(list_of_lists: Vec<Vec<Result<i32, Error>>>) -> Result<Vec<i32>, Error> {
    let mut flat = Vec::new();
    for entry in list_of_lists {
        for j in entry {
            flat.push(j?);
        }
    }
    Ok(flat)
}

We're flattening a list of lists, but each entry in the list may be an error. If we encounter such an error during flattening, we want to bail out immediately. We can't use extend here but it's pretty straightforward otherwise. 5

How about writing this with fold? If we do, the brilliant Rust clippy immediately suggest we use try_fold which is designed for error handling.

pub fn fallible_flatten_fold(
    list_of_lists: Vec<Vec<Result<i32, Error>>>,
) -> Result<Vec<i32>, Error> {
    list_of_lists
        .into_iter()
        .try_fold(Vec::new(), |accumulator, entry| {
            let mut result = accumulator.clone();
            for j in entry {
                result.push(j?);
            }
            Ok(result)
        })
}

If we ignore the performance difference which is inherent to folding over a collection like this, I'd still argue the for loop is easier to read and write in this scenario.

Conclusion

It's hard to go wrong with map() if what you're doing is transforming a collection.

But fold is a lot more tricky. Does that mean fold is useless? Not at all. I use fold in complex scenarios building up structures where a declarative route really pays off. Sometimes going up a level of abstraction allows you to do algorithmic improvements that blow even the performance of the for loop completely out of the water. But the humble for loop still has a lot of things going for it.

for loops have break. You can return from the middle of a for loop too. Complex error handling is expressed with a little ?.

To avoid for I could scratch my head a lot and go through a bigger catalog of concepts, and stretch my mathematical reasoning abilities. While there is definitely a time and place for that, in many cases the trade-offs for both the writer and reader of the code are in favor of the humble for loop, in Rust, as well. Let that inform the heuristics we use as programmers.

Update

I've published the project I used to do these measurements so others can replicate and criticize them.

@dinskid@mastodon.social had an interesting comment that got me thinking again. They asked about this:

let flat = flatten.into_iter().fold(Vec::new(), |mut accumulator, list| {
    acc.extend(list);
    acc
});

This is the same speed as the simple for loop. I had originally excluded this option as I had handled it in my JavaScript article as strictly worse: even though the performance is fine, mutating an argument is difficult to reason about, and it's not really functional anymore.

I didn't realize however that Rust changes these trade-offs as accumulator is a moved Vec and we know it's safe to modify it, as nothing else could possibly be referencing it. Yay for Rust! And thank you @dinskid@mastodon.social!

I still think the for loop is slightly easier to reason about, and it's somewhat easier to modify for the case of error handling. But there's not much to say against this option either.

1

I've used simple i32 integers for all experiments, and your performance will be different with different data types. Your results will vary depending on what you're looping through and what you're producing. Simple integers are the simplest for machines to handle.

2

When transforming a i32 to an f64 .map() is still a lot faster. When turning i32 into String the performance difference goes away.

3

Incidentally using extend was almost double the speed on my benchmark compared to an inner loop where stuff is manually pushed in an inner loop.

let mut flat = Vec::new();
for entry in list_of_lists {
    for j in entry {
        flat.push(j);
    }
}

Still super fast compared to the alternatives, but slower.

4

When you try flat_map(|list| list) the Rust linter (Clippy) springs into action suggesting you use flatten() instead. Bizarrely enough the flat_map approach on this simple benchmark is actually 30% faster.

5

Here's a way to use extend:

let e = entry.into_iter().collect::<Result<Vec<_>, _>>()?;
result.extend(e);

I suspect it's not faster as we have to instantiate the vector with collect() in order to filter out errors, but I haven't measured it.

item.description:

Thursday, 12 December 2024

New research, led by experts at the University of Nottingham, has found that repeated doses of paracetamol in people aged 65 and over, can lead to an increased risk of gastrointestinal, cardiovascular and renal complications.

The new study, which is published in Arthritis Care and Research, shows that care must be taken when repeated doses are required for chronic painful conditions such as osteoarthritis in older people.

The study was led by Professor Weiya Zhang, from the NIHR Biomedical Research Centre in the School of Medicine at the University of Nottingham.

Due to its perceived safety, paracetamol has long been recommended as the first line drug treatment for osteoarthritis by many treatment guidelines, especially in older people who are at higher risk of drug-related complications.”

The study analysed data from the Clinical Practice Research Datalink-Gold. Participants were aged 65 and over with an average age of 75, and had been registered with a UK GP practice for at least a year between 1998 and 2018.

Researchers looked at the health records of 180,483 people who had been prescribed paracetamol repeatedly (≥2 prescriptions within six months) during the study. Their health outcomes were then compared to 402,478 people of the same age who had never been prescribed paracetamol repeatedly.

The findings showed that prolonged paracetamol use was associated with an increased risk of peptic ulcers, heart failure, hypertension and chronic kidney disease.

Professor Zhang adds: “Whilst further research is now needed to confirm our findings, given its minimal pain-relief effect, the use of paracetamol as a first line pain killer for long-term conditions such as osteoarthritis in older people needs to be carefully considered.”

item.title: Bitbanging 1D Reversible Automata
item.description:
Score 94 | Comments 22 (thread link) | @richiejp
December 12, 2024 | https://richiejp.com/1d-reversible-automata | archive.org

One Dimensional Reversible Automata

I created a demo for the GFXPrim library. It implements and displays a nearest-neighbor, one-dimensional, binary cell automata. Additionally it implements a reversible automata, which is almost identical except for a small change to make it reversible. The automata is displayed over time in two dimensions, time travels from top to bottom. Although in the reversible case time could be played backwards.

The automata works as follows:

  • Each cell has a state, which is on or off, black or white, boolean etc.
  • At each time step, the state of a cell in the next step is chosen by a rule.
  • The rule looks at a cell’s current value and the values of its left and right neighbors.
  • There are 23 = 8 possible state combinations (patterns) for 3 binary cells.
  • A rule states which patterns result in a black cell in the next time step.
  • There are 28 = 256 possible rules. That is, 256 unique combinations of patterns.

So a pattern is a 3 digit binary number, where each digit corresponds to a cell. The middle digit is the center cell, the high order bit the left cell, the low order bit the right cell. A rule can be display by showing a row of patterns and a row of next states.

111 110 101 100 011 010 001 000
0 1 1 0 1 1 1 0

Above is rule 110, 0x6e or 01101110. It essentially says to match patterns 110, 101, 011, 010, 001. Where a pattern match results in the cell being set to 1 at the next time step. If no pattern is matched or equivalently, an inactive pattern is matched, then the cell will be set to 0.

Again note that each pattern resembles a 3bit binary number. Also the values of the active patterns resemble an 8bit binary number. We can use this to perform efficient matching of the patterns using binary operations.

Let’s assume our CPU natively operates on 64bit integers (called words). We can pack a 64 cell automata into a single 64bit integer. Each bit corresponds to a cell. If a bit is 1 then it is a black cell and 0 for white. In this case we are using integers as bit fields. We don’t care about the integer number the bits can represent.

The CPU can perform bitwise operations on all 64bits in parallel and without branching. This means we can perform a single operation 64 times in parallel.1

If we rotate (wrapped >>2) all bits to the right by one, then we get a new integer where the left neighbor of a bit is now in its position. Likewise if we shift all bits to the left, then we get an integer representing the right neighbors. This gives us 3 integers where the left, center and right bits are in the same position. For example, using only 8bits:

left: 0100 1011 >>
center: 1001 0110
right: 0010 1101 <<

Each pattern can be represented as a 3bit number, plus a 4th bit to say whether it is active in a given rule. As we want to operate on all 64bits at once in the left, right and center bit fields. We can generate 64bit long masks from the value of each bit in a given pattern.

So if we have a pattern where the left cell should be one, then we can create a 64bit mask of all ones. If it should be zero, then all zeroes. Likewise for the center and right cells. The masks can be xor’ed3 (^) with the corresponding cell fields to show if no match occurred. That is, if the pattern is one and the cell is zero or the cell is one and the pattern is zero. We can invert this (~) to give one when a match occurs.

To see whether all components (left, right, center) of a pattern matches we can bitwise and (&) them together. We can then bitwise or4 (|) the result of the pattern matches together to produce the final values.

If we wish to operate on an automata larger than 64 cells, then we can combine multiple integers into an array. After performing the left and right shifts, we get the high or low bit from the next or previous integers in the array. Then set the low and high bits of the right and left bit fields. In other words we chain them together using the end bits of the left and right bit fields.

For illustration purposes, below is the kernel of the the automata algorithm.

/* If bit n is 1 then make all bits 1 otherwise 0 */
#define BIT_TO_MAX(b, n) (((b >> n) & 1) * ~0UL)

/* Numeric representation of the current update rule */
static uint8_t rule = 110;

/* Apply the current rule to a 64bit segment of a row */
static inline uint64_t ca1d_rule_apply(uint64_t c_prev,
                                       uint64_t c,
                                       uint64_t c_next,
                                       uint64_t c_prev_step)
{
    int i;
    /* These are wrapping shifts when c_prev == c or c_next == c */
    uint64_t l = (c >> 1) ^ (c_prev << 63);
    uint64_t r = (c << 1) ^ (c_next >> 63);
    uint64_t c_next_step = 0;

    for (i = 0; i < 8; i++) {
        uint64_t active = BIT_TO_MAX(rule, i);
        uint64_t left   = BIT_TO_MAX(i, 2);
        uint64_t center = BIT_TO_MAX(i, 1);
        uint64_t right  = BIT_TO_MAX(i, 0);

        c_next_step |=
            active & ~(left ^ l) & ~(center ^ c) & ~(right ^ r);
    }

    /* The automata becomes reversible when we use c_prev_state */
    return c_next_step ^ c_prev_step;
}

To make the automata “reversible” an extra step can be added. We look at a cell’s previous (in addition to the current, left and right) and if it was one then invert the next value. This is equivalent to xor’ring the previous value with the next.

It is not entirely clear to me what the mathematical implications are of being reversible. However it is important to physics and makes some really cool patterns which mimic nature. Also entropy and the second rule of themodynamics, yada, yada…

The automata definition is taken from Stephen Wolfram’s “A new kind of science”. He proposes at least one obvious5 C implementation using arrays of cells. He also provides a table of binary expressions for each rule. E.g. rule 90 reduces to just the l^r binary expression. It may be possible for the compiler to automatically reduce my implementation to these minimal expressions.

To see why, let’s consider rule 90 for each pattern.

111 110 101 100 011 010 001 000
0 1 0 1 1 0 1 0

01011010 = 90

First for pattern 000.

  active & ~(left ^ l) & ~(center ^ c) & ~(right ^ r);
= 0 & ~(0 ^ l) & ~(0 ^ c) & ~(0 ^ r);
= 0.`

Active is zero so the whole line reduces to zero. Now for 001. Note that 1 here actually means ~0UL, that is 64bit integer max.

   1 & ~(0 ^ l) & ~(0 ^ c) & ~(1 ^ r);
= ~l & ~c & r.

As expected pattern 001 matches l=0, c=0, r=1. Let’s just list the remaining patterns or’ed together in their reduced state. Then reduce that further. Note that the for loop in ca1d_rule_apply will be unrolled by the compiler when optimising for performance. It’s also quite clear that c_next_step is dependant on an expression from the previous iteration or zero. So all the pattern match results will get or’ed together.

  l & c & ~r | l & ~c & ~r | ~l & c & r | ~l & ~c & r;
= l & ~r | ~l & r;
= l ^ r.

See on the top row that (l & c & ~r | l & ~c & ~r) or’s together c and not c. So we can remove it. Then we get an expression equivalent to xor’ring l and r.

In theory at least, the compiler can see that rule only has 256 values and create a reduced version of ca1d_rule_apply for each value. Whether it actually does is not of much practical concern when the rendering code is the bottle neck. However it’s interesting to see if the compiler can deduce the best solution or whether anything trips it up.

Judging from the disassembly from gcc -O3 -mcpu=native -mtune=native, it may actually do this. Additionally it vectorizes the code packing four 64bit ints at a time into 256bit registers and operating on those. I don’t know which part of the code it is vectorising or how. It’s possible that what I think is the rule being reduced is something related to vectorisation.

To render the automata we take the approach of iterating over each pixel in the image. We calculate which cell the pixel falls inside and set the color of the pixel to that of the cell. That’s it.

/* Draws a pixel */
static inline void shade_pixel(gp_pixmap *p, gp_coord x, gp_coord y,
                               gp_pixel bg, gp_pixel fg)
{
    gp_pixel px;
    size_t i = (x * (64 * width)) / p->w;
    size_t j = (y * height) / p->h;
    size_t k = 63 - (i & 63);
    uint64_t c = steps[gp_matrix_idx(width, j, i >> 6)];

    c = BIT_TO_MAX(c, k);
    px = (fg & c) | (bg & ~c);

    gp_putpixel_raw(p, x, y, px);
}

GFXPrim makes drawing very simple. The above code is fast enough for my purpsoses, but a significant improvement can be had. Integer division is much slower than floating point multiplication on most newer CPUs. It’s actually much faster (2x at least) on my CPU to calculate a pair of ratios in floating point, then convert them back to integers.

However, you may ask why we are even drawing on the CPU in the first place? This is because GFXPrim targets embedded systems with no graphics processor. Additionally the CPU may not even support floating point natively. So integer division may actually be faster in this case. Still better would be to limit the size of the pixmap to be 2x larger than the dimensions of the automata, where x ∈ ℕ then we can use shifts instead of division.

item.title: On AI for Developer Productivity
item.description:
Score 6 | Comments 0 (thread link) | @maisem
December 12, 2024 | https://mhlakhani.com/blog/2024/12/on-ai-for-productivity/ | archive.org

Some people say AI and LLMs will change the world and redefine how the software industry works. Others say it’s super overhyped and refuse to try it out or have tried it out and didn’t get any useful results. This will be my longest blog post ever, but I’ve been asked a few times about this topic, so I thought I’d write things down.

Disclaimer: This post isn’t intended to opine on the harms or benefits of AI in general. My thoughts on that topic would cover an equally long (if not longer) blog post, and I prefer to have a nuanced in-person discussion on that. I suggest reading this post from Nicholas Carlini, particularly the intro, nuance, and background sections - the author conveys things better than I can. If you haven’t read that post, you should also read it in full to understand how you can improve your productivity with AI.

Additional disclaimer: As with anything on this blog, views are purely my own, not those of my employer or anyone else I reference. Any mistakes here are also my own, and I’ll strive to correct them as I become aware.

TLDR: There are a lot of valid concerns around things like hallucinations. Due to those, until recently, I was staunchly in the “AI is just overhyped” camp. But, if a skilled operator is aware of and works around its limitations in the context of developer productivity, they can easily multiply their productivity by a factor of 3 or more. In this post, I’ll cover how I’ve used AI personally (including some use cases I haven’t seen elsewhere), what to watch out for, and what I’ve learned. I hope it’s useful!

Table of contents:

  • About me
  • How I use AI
    • Boutique developer tools
    • The grunt work part of the job
    • Agent-based systems for generating test data
    • Accelerating my productivity on side projects
    • Real examples from chat histories
    • Where I’ve tried to use AI and failed
  • Reflections
    • My mental model of AI
    • Properties of effective AI operators
    • Problems I think AI is well suited for
    • Things I don’t use AI for
    • Tips for getting started
    • I’m a student. Should I still bother learning to code?
  • Conclusion

About Me

For the briefest of my background, I’ve been writing code professionally for over a decade (and personally for over a decade before that). I was an absolute luddite and refused to use AI for a couple of years, but over the last year, I’ve started to use it a lot. A nontrivial part of my day job involves doing migrations and cleaning up tech debt. I like to call myself a code janitor, so anything that helps me write code more effectively is a win in my head.

A few relevant things (reasoning will become more apparent later):

  • Even before the advent of LLMs, I cared a lot about refining my craft and reducing overhead. My favorite example is how, at $past_job, during a large meeting, someone said they wished my team’s tool did X. During the meeting itself, I was able to build and submit a PR for that (admittedly minor) feature.
  • I’ve spent a lot of time mentoring and onboarding interns and junior engineers and have some intuition (through trial and error) about what works well and what doesn’t.

Recently, I’ve been quite involved in efforts at $work to improve developer productivity using AI where possible, and that’s part of my motivation for writing this post - to encourage others to at least try it.

Here is a smattering of things I’ve used AI for. This is primarily a descriptive section explaining problems I faced and how I’ve solved them using AI/LLMs. Reusing a quote from Nicholas Carlini again:

You may not like my use cases. You may think they're silly. It also may be the case that none of these relate to things that would help you. I accept this may be true. But I can only speak for myself.

My use cases have been roughly broken down into these categories (in ~rough order of usefulness to me)

  • Boutique/one-off developer tools for specific problems (I don’t see people talking about this often)
  • The ‘grunt work’ part of the job
  • Agent-based systems for generating/playing around with test data
  • Accelerating my productivity on side projects
  • Real examples from my chat history, e.g., understanding code, learning systems, etc.

I’m not going to spend too much time covering use cases that people commonly talk about (e.g., auto-complete in IDEs, etc). That’s been written to death. Suffice it to say I do use Copilot autocomplete, Copilot Edits (as of last week), Cursor for side projects (recently), Replit Agent (tried it a bit!), and chat with Claude and ChatGPT to brainstorm ideas.

Boutique developer tools

PS: I don’t see people writing about this enough. If I’ve missed examples (I probably have), please let me know.

One of my biggest revelations has been that I can just use AI to write tools which I have always wished I had to get my job done faster.

Example 1: “online migration”

Earlier this year, at $dayjob, I got involved in an effort to clean up some tech debt. Without going into much detail, it can be considered an online migration/dual write strategy (e.g., described here). We had data structure A, added data structure B, and wanted to ensure that A == B across many services.

So we did the standard thing, added instrumentation at places A was used, compared it to B, and logged a stack trace + the values of A and B where they differed. And then tried to update the code to ensure they matched. Using standard logging tools to view these (e.g., ELK) got extremely tedious.

Knowing I’d be working on this for a while, I decided to try and optimize my workflow. So, in one day, I built a tool that queried our logging system for a given service, looked up all the relevant logs, categorized them by type of difference, and pretty-printed output. So I could see e.g., service X has N issues, of which the majority are this one stack trace. Then I could drill down, see the stack trace, have it filter out irrelevant frames, color code relevant frames as red/green/blue, and point me to the appropriate code to fix.

I spent about six months working on this problem personally (not discounting others who worked on this effort). This tool saved me at least a few hours per investigation, and I would easily say it’s saved me a few hundred hours of work in aggregate. Would I have built this without AI? No. Was it worth spending one day doing this? Absolutely.

While I can’t show that magical tool, I can show an auxiliary tool I built. It would take one specific request, trace it through various services, and let me browse without leaving a terminal. Here is a demo where I’ve replaced service names and stack traces with fake data.

NB: Yes, some presentation bugs are now showing up. This is the pitfall of AI-generated code, and I just broke some things when stubbing out data.

Again, never in my life would I have imagined writing a curses-based UI to process text. And here I am.

Example 2: Scaffolding for migrations

I often work on migrations and code cleanups. While each migration is unique (I could write a long post on migrations), there’s usually some standard boilerplate. Picking just one example – I did a migration where we switched from one cache type to an instrumented cache type, which did some logging.

The changes were primarily mechanical, e.g., replace new Cache[K,V]() { /\* lambda for loadKey */ } with makeInstrumentedCache[K, V]() { /* different lambda for loadKey */ } (well, a little more complex so I couldn’t just find and replace). I did the following:

  • Used AI to help me write a scalafix codemod
  • Then wrote a script to orchestrate it, which:
    • Searched for all instances of the old pattern
    • Grouped by folder/top-level service and then for each service:
    • Created a new git branch
    • Ran the migration
    • Ensured the code compiled
    • Committed the changes
    • Submitted a PR for review

On its own, it’s unclear if that adds value - I could have done that by hand. How much time did I save? maybe a few minutes per PR?

But this adds up. For just that migration alone, I did about 20-something PRs. I’ve used this for hundreds of PRs since. But what’s more important is that it runs autonomously. I can run this on my machine, cranking out PRs while in a meeting or at lunch.

The grunt work part of the job

We’ve all run into this. There’s some boilerplate task you want to do that no one cares about - sometimes I’d honestly feel bad even handing that to an intern - but AI steps up and gets the job done.

Here are a few examples where it added up for me.

In one project, I had to take table schemas from a design doc and translate them into CREATE TABLE statements (nobody’s got time to copy over 100 columns, their types, and comments).

In another project, I had to orchestrate calling a vendor tool. The vendor tool had a .yaml file to configure it, while I wanted to write a protobuf API for callers of my service to invoke it. I copy-pasted the vendor's documentation, asked AI to write me a protobuf file mirroring the semantics, and then asked it to translate from the protobuf to the yaml so I could call the vendor tool.

For one project, I had to collect and label a lot of project-specific data. I ended up using AI in a couple of ways to help out:

  • We had a few hundred entries to classify/rank in terms of importance and some documents/spreadsheets covering various subsets of data that I was given as reference/prior art. I tossed it all at Claude (the documents contained the ranking plus reasoning as to why), asked it to give me a JSON mapping from the entry to its classification, and looked at all the results. They mostly made sense.
  • I had to review hundreds of source code files to understand whether a tool’s definition matched ours. Reading through hundreds of source files to know where they did and didn’t match was super tedious. I worked with an expert to get an understanding of the definitions, tossed each file plus that prompt at an LLM and asked it to categorize and explain the reasoning, and put the results into a sheet. Then, I could eyeball and check that each result was correct while quickly looking at the source files to verify.

I literally procrastinated on this for a few weeks - having something to start in the correct format was much more manageable. The cost of getting it wrong was also low: I was looking at all the results (and fixed a few entries), I had someone else review the results (also fixed a few entries), and *if* we did get something wrong (we would look at the data from this system manually anyway), it would take about a minute to just re-classify all entries.

These are examples where the work is not hard. It’s just mind-numbingly tedious or annoying to start, and if you’re like me, when you get to this state, you will procrastinate and put things off forever. It’s also near the start of a project, so you often just never get started. Getting over this hump has been an immense productivity boost for me.

Agent-based systems for generating test data

On the side, I help with UpliftAI (it’s a great initiative; you should look it up).

A few months ago, I helped with model training and cost optimization. At the time, we were working async, and I needed to build code/pipelines to train the model and got blocked because we were waiting for our team to provide a good ground truth dataset.

Rather than wait, I did what seemed obvious and generated fake data I could use to ensure my code worked end to end, so that I could just run it when the real data showed up.

I brainstormed with Hammad and built an agentic system to generate the needed data. This was my first time doing it, and within just an hour and a half, I had a lot of sample data for under 10 cents (enough to unblock my coding).

I asked Claude to generate a system of AI agents to generate this data. I’ll leave the code out, but here’s the description of the approach it gave me in the first response - which worked quite well after I iterated on it a few times:

This approach uses a chain of specialized LLM agents to generate a diverse and relevant dataset for your [ redacted ] model. Here's a brief explanation of how to implement this:

  1. Set up each agent as a separate function or class, using an LLM (like GPT-4) with appropriate prompts.
  2. Create a simple orchestration script that feeds the output of one agent into the next.
  3. Start with the Persona Generator Agent, creating a diverse set of Pakistani personas.
  4. Feed these personas into the Utterance Generator Agent to create raw utterances.
  5. Use the Dialogue Flow Agent to create multi-turn conversations from these utterances.
  6. Pass the generated content through the Labeling and Categorization Agent for proper tagging.
  7. Use the Quality Control Agent to review and filter the content.
  8. Finally, use the Dataset Compiler Agent to structure the final dataset.

Pre-AI and LLMs, I would have just waited a few more weeks and been hard-blocked on that data set. But with these, I was able to unblock myself. I also learned about the power of agent-based systems.

Since the first draft of this post, I also saw this announcement from $work and now I wish I had seen it earlier - would’ve saved so much time!

Accelerating my productivity on side projects

For me, side projects are, by definition, projects where:

  • I want to work on them.
  • I don’t have enough time to work on them, and when I do, it’s sporadic
  • I have ideas, but they come and go in bursts
  • I don’t have anyone to bounce ideas off of / check my work

AI is helpful here as a buddy to get things done.

Recently, I added a feature to my reading list archive to make it easier to share links. I’d been putting it off forever since I hadn’t touched the code in a while. I didn’t have much time (under 30 minutes), so I’d usually give up and never start. But in this case, I just asked Cursor to do it: “Add the capability to publish all unpublished posts on this results page in one button click.” - it got through most of the boilerplate, had one bug, which I was able to fix, and then I could be on my merry way.

I’ve used AI to help get over the initial hump and get started on projects - e.g., I am terrible at frontend/graphics work but have always wanted to make a game (excited by the game design principles). So I got it to help me with boilerplate graphics code and debugging coordinate systems (I had an off-by-half-tile error I spent over a day on), which let me focus on the fun part of building my game.

I’ve used AI to get me over the hump for things I don’t always want to do that are nonetheless important - e.g. writing documentation. I did that for rocket_csrf_guard as I wanted to have documentation ready before open sourcing. I vetted all the documentation, but it’s much faster to edit and review and fix documentation than it is to start writing from scratch with writer’s block. And again, without that, I wouldn’t have open sourced it, and then I wouldn’t have been able to write this blog post explaining a security idea which others found valuable.

I’ve also used AI to brainstorm ideas, toss stupid ideas back and forth, and have it shoot them down, which is helpful when I’m too scared of sounding like an idiot to a human. It helps tell me what I need to let me search for well-sourced material. The best part is that I can use the otherwise unproductive time for this - there’s time on the train/during a walk where I’d usually just zone out, but now I can send one question, zone out, and check back in a while and fire off another question and repeat.

I’ve tried Replit Agent to build some prototypes from scratch, and it got close, but not quite there. You can see more in a prior LinkedIn post. However, it was great, as I could code on my phone on the go (similar to the above).

Lastly, most recently, I’ve started using AI to review my code—the SNR is up and down, but it’s better than no one reviewing my code. Hopefully, I’ll have more to share about this soon.

Real examples from my chat histories

Here are real examples of things I’ve had AI do for me, taken from Copilot / Cursor / ChatGPT / Claude histories. I haven’t included the entire back-and-forth conversations for everything but have left commentary at least early on. Hopefully, this gives a flavor for the types of tasks I’ve found it helpful for. Note that this is an unordered, brain-dump style list.

Copilot

1. For this post itself, I used AI to generate dummy data for that tool (this was my third attempt at this prompt):

I'm trying to do a demo and want to hide private information. Please change query_logs to instead return 30 rows of dummy data, with each row being a bit diverse, and reusing some service names. Generate realistic looking log messages though, and make them have potentially long stacktraces with realistic looking function names in Scala.

2. I had a test script for some work, and it was annoying to depend on a third party library whenever I used it on a new machine. So:

Rewrite this code to only use the python standard library so that I don't need to import 'requests'

3. I wanted to debug a part of that script and share a one-liner with others to test. So:

Give me a curl command I can run to mimic this_redacted_function

4. The initial prompt I used to build the script shown in the demo above:

I'm trying to write a python tool to debug some logs. Please write me something where I can give it a keyword, then it will query the log system (assume I have that part written) and then parse the results and display them in an interactive CLI tool, with one short line per row. It should let me use my arrow keys to go up and down and expand/contract lines to view the full messages.

5. Day-to-day coding cleanups:

The last 3 tests in this file have a lot of duplicated code. Could you please write a helper function and factor out the boilerplate?

6. Some code from last week where I couldn’t be bothered to write a parser:

I am trying to write an error parser for some scala error messages. Write me a function that takes a string like the one below, and returns a map from the filepath to the list of errors in there. Note that each error block is 5 lines long if it helps

That seems wrong? The first block that describes the actual error doesn't actually start with [error] right?

7. Related to the above - it is good at translating across languages:

I'm trying to port the error parsing code in this Scala file to python3. Please give me a function that parses the error file given a path, and returns structured information about the error (different dataclasses for each error), generally following the structure in the attached file.

8. I was on-call and trying to quickly unblock some team that was having issues with Kubernetes access. I suspected the problem was in their code and not in my system, but I don’t know much about Kubernetes. So, I asked Copilot to translate their code to a kubectl command so I could confirm it worked directly, and it did:

Please convert redacted_function_name to a series of kubectl commands I can run directly

ChatGPT / Claude

1. Learning about various arcane minutiae of commonly known tools/code syntax:

given a path to a file, what bazel command can I use to tell me which target owns it?

I have a bazel target in a specific folder. How can I query the set of targets that directly depend on it that also live in the same folder?

I have a json object like the one below. Write me a jq expression that gets me all the values of the value key for the variable in the environment

I have a server running on a specific ip and port. How can I use nmap to confirm which versions of TLS it supports?

I am using comby, a static analysis tool that lets me analyze protobuf files. Please help me write a match expression that matches the use of a message type. My goal is to figure out which messages are still used in a protobuf file and which ones may be unused.

2. Various dumb coding questions so I can get started:

How can I HMAC a string in Java and encode the output as a Base64 string?

Write me a python script which searches a directory (with directories in it) for SPECIAL_STRING and lists out the files that contain it, grouped by the top level directory

Write some scala code that converts from lower_case_with_underscores to camelCase

how can I fix this scala 2.13 compiler error? [ insert complex one I’d never seen before ]

I am trying to clean up my scala codebase and migrate from an older API to a new one. Please write me a syntactic scalafix rule which identifies calls to OldApi.create that only have one argument passed, and rewrites those to additionally have an argument newFlag=true. Just give me the scala code.

The python code below is really slow. Make it faster.

this is extremely slow spark code, how can I speed it up? I have a list of arrays in my python code that I want to use to update a spark dataframe

I have the following SQL query which returns many rows, including multiple rows for each primary_key. Please update it so I can have a table which contains exactly one row per primary_key, using the fields from the earliest value of found_at for each row when grouped by the primary_key. But use the latest resolved_time

3. Brainstorming side project ideas: (picking one of the dozens of chats here)

I am thinking of writing a cricket management game similar to Cricket Captain or Football Manager. Which functionality do you think would be enjoyable for the average mobile gamer interested in cricket?

Where I’ve tried to use AI and failed

It’s not all fun and games. There were many prompts/dead ends where I used AI and gave up. Here are a few I thought were illustrative.

While working on my game, I thought I’d be lazy and see if I could get Copilot to write the pathfinding. Correctness matters there, but surely it had enough examples in its training set and I could test it out to see if it worked, right? Wrong. It had a couple of subtle off-by-one errors (one sign flip, one place it did a < instead of a <=) that only showed up in edge cases (rounding!). I learned my lesson, went back to a textbook and refreshed my memory on how to write these. And probably for the better.

Given that I do many migrations, I decided to also try AI just to do the whole migration for me rather than using it to aid in writing e.g., a static analysis-based migration. I haven’t quite been able to make it work, and I’ve had three failed 1-day hackathons for various reasons (files being too large, hallucinating line numbers in patches, etc.). However, there is a silver lining for this one: I got over some of these roadblocks during the latest hackathon at $work (just last week). I'm hoping to share more soon once I finalize my approach and run it on a few more examples to confirm it generalizes.

Before reading this, please read the disclaimer at the top. Again, I’m recapping my personal experience and the lessons I’ve learned here —I cannot speak definitively.

My mental model of AI

I think of AI as an intern who:

  • Has encyclopedic knowledge (memorized facts about almost everything) => so I can ask them about anything, and they’ll know something.
  • Has predominantly been exposed to rote learning and not deep thought => so they might know how to do a well-specified task, but they cannot explain their train of thought or handle unfamiliar problems, and I need to be careful with assignments
  • Has amnesia and doesn’t remember what I told them an hour ago => so I always need to teach them from scratch
  • Is eager to impress => so they will always politely and confidently respond with something, even if it’s absolutely wrong.
  • Is drunk and/or high and gets things wrong half the time => so I always need to triple-check their work and never give them anything mission-critical

Going in with this set of assumptions has helped me change how I view AI and get a lot more out of it.

Properties of effective AI operators

These are some common properties I’ve seen in others who’ve used AI to greatly enhance their productivity (and then some hints of it subsequently in myself, though not to that level). I make no claims whether these are necessary or sufficient - just pointing out a correlation.

  • They are experienced mentors. They have trained multiple interns and other engineers, so they know how to phrase questions, how to be critical of someone’s work, and how to see past answers that only seem correct.
  • They value their craft and tools. They’ve honed their craft (e.g., toolchain, dev environment, etc.) and take pride in the quality and efficiency of their work. AI is just another tool for improving themselves.
  • They are damn good at what they do. They know a lot of deep technical domains in and out, so they know when an answer is plausible and worth exploring more or when the AI is sending them down a dead end. They know how to test/validate responses.

Problems I think AI is well suited for

From my experience (and you might have figured this out given the examples), I think the most important thing is, “does it matter if the thing I build is not 100% correct”? If not, I potentially look into AI. If yes, I ask myself, “is it easy for me to validate that the answer is 100% correct?”. If yes, I’ll potentially look into AI. If not, well, this is a problem that’s not suitable for AI at this time for me (see next section).

There are a few other things I ask myself when deciding:

  • Is it something I hate doing? I’ll use AI to get over the equivalent of writer’s block.
  • Am I doing something hundreds of people have done before? If so, I’ll use AI - it’s likely to have memorized a technical solution.
  • Is it some technical minutiae, like the right syntax for a bazel command? I’ll try it out. Worst case, the AI gets it wrong, and I lose ten seconds.
  • Am I the only primary user of this result/thing? If so, I have a lower quality bar for things for myself. If it helps me with my workflow, I’ll try it out.

Things I don’t use AI for

Note that this doesn’t distinguish between “I’ll never use AI for this” and “I won’t use AI for this just yet.” and “I just am not smart enough to have gotten this to work”.

First and foremost, if I’m working on a problem where correctness matters and I can’t readily validate that the AI solution is correct (because it’s hard to test automatically, or I don’t know enough about the domain), I start running away from it. I care about getting things right. So this means I avoid using AI for any security-related work, or systems building work. And that’s OK. I do enough other work, such that using AI lets me save my mental energy for when correctness does matter.

Beyond that:

  • Anything requiring super complex reasoning (I haven’t gotten it to work)
  • Things that require multi-shot, complex agent systems (I just haven’t yet found an effective workflow that I can use at $work)
  • Anything requiring larger context windows (e.g., I can migrate small snippets of code, but nothing significant).
  • Writing. It’s a sacred art form to me. I will sometimes use it to critique my writing (though I’m more likely to use Grammarly, which I also often disregard because it cramps my style), but every word on my blog is artisanally hand-crafted by me.
  • Reading. Reading is also sacred. If you know me, you know I read a lot. I don’t want to read an AI-generated summary. I will read the whole thing so I can form my own opinions (yes, I realize there’s a contradiction between this and the existence of algorithmic feeds).

Tips for getting started

Honestly, the biggest tip is just to try it out. I tried it out a few times and gave up because it sucked. But then it improved, and I gave it a more serious try and tried a few more things before it all clicked for me.

Understand the problems it works well for and where it doesn’t. Don’t apply it to the wrong thing, or you will get frustrated at the lack of results.

This will sound like a cop-out or gatekeeper-y, but I highly recommend working on your core skills first. You can do okay and improve using AI, but it takes skill to know whether it’s wasting your time or not. Improving your mentorship skills will help you be a better person in general, too. Most importantly, though, start caring a lot about the quality of your work and be proud of it. Once you strive to improve however you can, you’ll realize AI is just one of many tools you can use on that journey.

I’m a student. Should I still bother learning to code?

I need a better answer here. Only time can tell. But here are my initial thoughts.

If you’re a junior engineer/student reading this, I recommend trying out AI and learning. You’ll be asked about how you can use AI when you apply for jobs. Focus on the fundamentals (assuming AI doesn’t exist - except for say, learning). Sure, you can use AI to write solutions for your assignments, but you won’t learn how things work - which will only harm you in the long term. Get your fundamentals right, and then use AI to supercharge your skills. in short, I recommend - technically:

  • Knowing your language of choice very well
  • Being an expert at data structures / algorithms
  • Debugging (vastly underrated skill in general)
  • Always asking “why” - don’t take the answer as a given if you ask AI for an explanation - try to understand the concept behind it, why something works a given way, etc

In a world with AI I expect “soft” skills (I hate this term) to be much more important even for junior engineers:

  • Knowing how to work as part of a team
  • Understanding what you need to build and why
  • Time management and prioritization
  • Communication
  • Planning
  • Note-taking
  • Learning from others, and teaching others
  • Context switching

I could go on, but that’s the rough gist (and I’ll try to get back to blogging about those at some point)

This was a really long post. I don’t have a solid conclusion. I will just say:

  • Try AI and see if it works for you.
  • Be conscious of and correct for the cases when it can get things wrong
  • Focus on honing your craft and your skills - AI hasn’t changed that

If you’ve read this far - thank you! As always I welcome any feedback or suggestions.
